extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in introductory proofs / discrete mathematics / first advanced mathematics course
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for constructing and presenting mathematical proofs (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, existence/uniqueness, set proofs), aimed at beginning undergraduate students learning rigorous proof techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by assuming the negation of the statement to be proved, deduce a contradiction, and conclude the original statement is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any statement that is clearly false is sufficient as the contradiction (examples given: 2 = 2 would not be a contradiction but 2 = 4 or 4 | 2 would be). Illustrative examples: Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes; the sin x + cos x ≥ 1 example. Use the equivalence ¬(∀x P(x)) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) when appropriate to produce a specific witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction for conditional statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'If P, then Q' by contradiction, assume both P and ¬Q, then derive a contradiction (C ∧ ¬C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline given: 'Suppose P and ∼Q. ... Therefore C ∧ ∼C.' Example: proving 'if a^2 is even then a is even' begins with 'suppose a^2 is even and a is not even' and derives a contradiction. Use this template directly when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradiction works well for universal statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof by contradiction is often effective for statements of the form ∀x, P(x) because ¬(∀x, P(x)) is equivalent to ∃x, ¬P(x), giving a specific x to work with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduction to an existential statement frequently supplies a concrete witness that leads to the contradiction; example: assume ∃x in an interval such that sin x + cos x < 1 and derive contradiction using that x's properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct or contrapositive over contradiction when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proof by contradiction only when direct or contrapositive methods do not seem to work, because contradiction proofs can hide a simpler contrapositive or direct proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a proof that assumed 'a2 − 2a + 7 is even and a is not odd' effectively did the contrapositive; a clearer, more efficient presentation used the contrapositive directly. The text advises looking for the simpler approach first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining techniques (proofs inside proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable and common to combine different proof techniques within a single proof (e.g., begin with a direct proof, and use contradiction or contrapositive for a sub-claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such 'proofs inside proofs' are normal: e.g., an overall direct proof of 'r is a product of two irrationals' contained a subproof by contradiction showing r/√2 is irrational. The textbook warns to be careful and explicit about scope and assumptions of nested proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for If-and-Only-If (biconditional) proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'P if and only if Q' prove both conditional directions: P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P (each may use direct, contrapositive, or contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin a new paragraph when starting the proof of the converse (Q ⇒ P). It is recommended to begin the second paragraph with the word 'Conversely' and to remind the reader which statement that paragraph is proving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving equivalence of multiple statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a list of statements are equivalent, prove a chain of implications that connects them circularly (or use other patterns that pairwise imply each other) so that truth of one forces truth of all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A circular pattern (a⇒b⇒c⇒...⇒a) yields the fewest implications to prove. Other patterns (mix of ⇐⇒ and ⇒) are acceptable. Each conditional in the pattern can be proved by any standard method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence proofs (∃x R(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove an existence statement, provide a specific example (witness) x for which R(x) holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often a single explicit example suffices, but sometimes verification is required to show the example indeed satisfies R(x) (the text notes that just asserting the example without verification is incomplete).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence proofs embedded in conditionals (construct witness depending on parameters)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an existence statement is inside a universal conditional (e.g., ∀a,b ∃k,ℓ such that ...), construct the witness(s) k,ℓ explicitly as functions of the given parameters or produce them via an algorithmic/structural argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proving existence of integers k,ℓ with gcd(a,b) = ak + bℓ used the set A = {ax+by : x,y ∈ Z}, selected its smallest positive element d, then showed d = ak + bℓ and that d = gcd(a,b). This uses well-ordering/minimal-element reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'there exists a unique x such that P(x)', first produce an example d with P(d), then assume any other candidate d' satisfying P and show d' = d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook's pattern: show d' ≤ d and d ≤ d' (or otherwise deduce equality) to conclude uniqueness. The gcd characterization example demonstrates this pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive versus non-constructive existence proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish whether a proof actually constructs an explicit witness (constructive) or merely proves existence without producing a concrete example (non-constructive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example non-constructive proof: show that either √2^√2 is rational or else (√2^√2)^√2 = 2 is rational without deciding which case holds. Constructive example: give explicit irrational x,y (x=√2, y=log_2 9) and prove x^y = 3 (rational). The text advises being alert to the distinction in reading and writing proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to show membership a ∈ A (set-builder proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is given as {x : P(x)}, show P(a) is true. If A = {x ∈ S : P(x)}, verify a ∈ S and show P(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several worked examples demonstrate checking both the domain condition and the predicate, and exemplify common mistakes (e.g., negative integers not fitting a specified domain).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove A ⊆ B (direct and contrapositive templates)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove A ⊆ B, prove the conditional 'if a ∈ A then a ∈ B' (direct approach) or equivalently prove the contrapositive 'if a ∉ B then a ∉ A'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct approach template: 'Suppose a ∈ A. ... Therefore a ∈ B. Hence A ⊆ B.' Contrapositive template: 'Suppose a ∉ B. ... Therefore a ∉ A. Hence A ⊆ B.' The text notes you may also use contradiction by assuming a ∈ A ∧ a ∉ B and deriving contradiction. Examples: divisibility subsets (18|x implies 6|x) and intersections implying divisibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctly negate compound and quantified statements
rubrics_metrics.description: When using contradiction, correctly apply logical negations (DeMorgan's laws and quantifier negation): e.g., ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q and ¬(∀x P(x)) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text example: negating 'a divides b or a divides (b+1)' leads (by DeMorgan) to 'a | b and a | (b+1)' during the setup of a contradiction proof. Proper logical transformation is crucial to set up the correct assumptions (and to obtain a usable witness when negating universals).

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes a valid contradiction (practical examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any statement that is clearly false under the current assumptions suffices to conclude contradiction; the exact form may vary depending on the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: deriving '1/ pk is an integer' vs '1/pk is not an integer', showing both 'a2 is even' and 'a2 is not even', or concluding 'a ≥ 2 and a < 2' are acceptable contradictions. The book emphasizes that the contradiction need not be a single canonical form.
